node.responsibility: Determine whether a shape has been divided into equal-sized parts, and divide given shapes into a specified number of equal parts.
node.academicBoundary: Limit to partitioning simple shapes (squares, rectangles, circles, bars) into 2, 3, 4, or 6 equal parts. Do not introduce fraction notation or naming of parts yet. Do not compare fractions or use denominators larger than 6.
node.evidenceGoal: Student correctly identifies equal vs. unequal partitions across at least 4 examples and correctly partitions at least 3 new shapes into a specified number of equal parts.

artifact.title: Fair Slice Bakery
artifact.audienceRationale: Reina's data shows sustained, low-frustration engagement with high-volume, fast-cycle precision tasks (spell-check: 167 plays, 100% accuracy, 0.99 engagement, 0.10 frustration; word-radar: 112 plays, 0.86 engagement) rather than novelty-driven spinners she tried briefly. She thrives on rapid rounds where she can self-check correctness immediately and rack up reps. This node design leans into that pattern: short, snappy rounds with instant visual feedback on a physical-feeling cutting task, letting her build volume and mastery the way she already prefers, while the drag-to-cut mechanic adds tactile novelty absent from her prior word-based activities.
artifact.openingPromise: Every customer at your bakery wants a fair share — cut wrong, and someone gets cheated. Cut right, and the whole town lines up for your pastries.
artifact.firstThreeSeconds: A single round cookie sits on a cutting board with one knife-drag line already shown as a demo, splitting it into two obviously unequal pieces — a customer's face frowns and a red X flashes over the cut.
artifact.firstAction: Reina drags her finger across the cookie to make a straight cut; the moment she releases, the two resulting pieces are outlined and she sees instantly whether they match in size.
artifact.interactionDemonstration: Before the first real order, a 2-second animated hand drags a bad cut (uneven halves, customer frowns) then a good cut (even halves, customer smiles), showing the exact same gesture she'll use.
artifact.coreInteraction: Each order ticket shows a shape (square, rectangle, circle, or bar) and a number of pieces needed (2, 3, 4, or 6). Reina drags cut lines onto the shape to divide it. An overlay meter shows live piece-size comparison as she drags. On release, pieces are shaded in matched colors if equal, mismatched colors with a wobble if not. She also gets quick 'Yes/No' judgment tickets: a pre-cut shape appears and she taps a green checkmark or red X to judge if the cuts are fair before any customer is served.
artifact.mathAsPower: Precise cutting is the only way to keep the bakery's reputation alive — she is using equal partitioning as a real tool to satisfy customers, not an abstract exercise. Fraction notation is deliberately absent; the power is purely visual-spatial: seeing and creating true equality.
artifact.stakes: A rotating cast of customers wait in line with a patience bar. A fair cut earns coins and a happy customer sprite; an unfair cut makes the customer huffy and the patience bar for the whole line drops slightly.
artifact.consequences: Three unfair cuts in a row temporarily 'closes' the bakery for a short cooldown (10 seconds) where she watches the line grumble and shrink — low-stakes but visually clear feedback, no failure state that blocks progress.
artifact.recovery: After any wrong cut, the shape resets instantly with a faint ghost outline showing where the equal cut lines should have gone, and she can immediately re-attempt the same order for full coins, so mistakes cost time, not standing.
progression: Level 1: Judge-only tickets — tap check or X on pre-made cuts into halves and thirds (equal vs unequal recognition).
Level 2: Guided cutting — cut simple bars and rectangles into 2 or 4 equal parts with snap-guides faintly visible.
Level 3: Free cutting — cut squares and circles into 2, 3, 4, or 6 equal parts with no guides, judged by the live size meter.
Level 4: Mixed rush hour — alternating judge tickets and free-cut orders across all shapes and part-counts, timed for bakery 'rush' with bonus coins for streaks.
artifact.worldReaction: The bakery's storefront visually fills with more customers, string lights, and new pastry displays as her fair-cut streak grows; a grumpy line and dim lights appear if her accuracy dips, giving constant ambient feedback beyond just per-round scoring.
artifact.payoff: At the end of a rush-hour session, the bakery is shown fully lit and packed with satisfied customer sprites holding perfectly even slices, and she unlocks a new pastry skin (cake, pie, baguette) to cut in the next session.
artifact.replayVariation: Each replay randomizes shape type, required piece count (2, 3, 4, or 6), and orientation of the shape (rotated bars, off-center circles) so identical cuts don't repeat, plus occasional 'trickster' pre-cut tickets with subtly unequal pieces to sharpen discrimination.
artifact.visualDirection: Warm, clean bakery palette (cream, pastel pink, caramel) with bold high-contrast outlines on shapes so cut lines and piece boundaries are unambiguous; customer sprites are simple and expressive (round, Duolingo-owl-adjacent but original) to keep focus on the shape itself.
artifact.motionDirection: Cut lines animate as a smooth, slightly elastic knife-drag with a satisfying snap when a cut is confirmed; equal pieces gently separate and settle with a soft bounce, unequal pieces jitter/wobble briefly to signal imbalance without harsh shake.
artifact.soundDirection: Soft chime on correct equal cut, a low thud/buzz (non-punitive) on unequal cut, ambient bakery sounds (light chatter, oven ding) that swell as the streak grows, quiet during cooldown to signal a pause rather than punishment.
usefulLibraries: Konva.js or Fabric.js for draggable cut-line rendering and shape geometry
Matter.js (lightweight) for piece separation/bounce physics on cut confirmation
GSAP for smooth cut-line, wobble, and customer-reaction animations
Howler.js for layered ambient/feedback sound management
artifact.engagementPrediction: High: the fast-cycle, self-checking, low-verbal-load format mirrors the exact conditions (spell-check, word-radar) where Reina showed her highest engagement and lowest frustration, while the drag-to-cut mechanic offers fresh tactile novelty distinct from her word-based history.
artifact.falsifyingEvidence: If Reina's completion rate drops sharply on free-cutting levels (Level 3+) or frustrationScore-equivalent behaviors (rapid retries without progress, early exits) appear specifically when guides are removed, this would indicate the spatial precision demand exceeds her current comfort zone and guided-cut support should be extended longer before full free-cutting is introduced.

node.responsibility: Identify and represent a unit fraction (1/b) as exactly one of b equal parts of a whole, and connect the fraction symbol to the shaded/selected part.
node.academicBoundary: Restrict to unit fractions only (numerator of 1) with denominators 2 through 8. Do not address non-unit fractions (e.g., 2/3) or fraction comparison. Do not use improper fractions or mixed numbers.
node.evidenceGoal: Student correctly shades or selects one part matching a given unit fraction in at least 4 new examples (e.g., shape divided into fifths, sixths, eighths) and correctly writes the unit fraction for at least 3 shaded models.

artifact.title: Lantern Keeper: One Pane of Many
artifact.audienceRationale: Reina's evidence shows very high volume and completion on short, precise, scan-and-mark tasks (167/167 spell-check at 1.00 accuracy, 112/112 word-radar at 0.655 accuracy with engagement 0.859). She finishes what she starts and tolerates being wrong in a scanning context, but her frustration rises there (0.271), so this design keeps the 'scan and mark exactly one target' rhythm she repeats voluntarily while making every miss visually diagnosable rather than merely wrong. Each round is a single decisive tap or a single symbol written — short loops she can stack many of — and correctness is confirmed by the world lighting up, not by a scolding buzzer. Her spotless accuracy record on a checking task also suggests she enjoys being the authority who verifies; the second half of this node lets her be the one who writes the label the world then obeys.
artifact.openingPromise: You are the keeper of a lighthouse whose glass is cut into equal panes. Light exactly one pane — the right one — and a ship finds its way home.
artifact.firstThreeSeconds: A dark harbor. A single lighthouse lamp housing floats center-screen, its round glass already scored into 4 equal wedges, all dim. One wedge pulses faintly with a warm amber glow, and a small brass plate below the glass reads 1/4. A ship's bell taps once.
artifact.firstAction: Tap the one pulsing wedge. It ignites amber, a beam sweeps the harbor, and the first ship's lamp answers from the dark. No instructions needed — one thing is glowing, tap it.
artifact.interactionDemonstration: Round 1 is guided: only the correct pane pulses, so the tap is guaranteed. Round 2 removes the pulse but keeps a ghost outline tracing the correct pane once, slowly, then fading — the student sees the finger-path before making it. Round 3 onward the student is on their own. Above the lamp, a persistent brass rail shows the anatomy of the label as the student works: the bottom number of 1/4 briefly enlarges and the four panes each flash once in sequence (four panes = bottom number), then the top number enlarges and exactly one pane holds its glow (light one). This anatomy replay is available on demand from a small lever, forever, without penalty.
artifact.coreInteraction: Two alternating modes inside one world. MODE A — LIGHT THE PANE: a lamp housing appears divided into b equal parts (b = 2 through 8) in one of several shapes — round glass, rectangular window frame, hexagonal signal lantern, long horizontal bar-lamp on the pier. A brass plate states a unit fraction such as 1/6. The student taps exactly one pane to light it. Tapping a second pane extinguishes the first, so 'exactly one' is enforced by the physics of the lamp rather than by an error message. A confirm-lever locks the choice. MODE B — ENGRAVE THE PLATE: a lamp already has exactly one pane lit; the brass plate is blank. The student builds the fraction by dragging brass numeral tiles into two slots stacked over a fraction bar, or taps a numeral wheel. To confirm, they pull the lever and the plate stamps. Crucially, in Mode B the world checks the student's engraving by acting on it: a second identical lamp, dark, obeys the engraved plate and lights that many-th of itself — if the plate says 1/6 the twin lamp splits into six and lights one, and the student sees whether the twin matches the original. Some Mode A rounds include distractor lamps whose glass is divided into unequal panes; these cannot be lit at all (they spark and stay dark), quietly reinforcing node 1's equal-parts rule without teaching it again.
artifact.mathAsPower: The denominator is the count of equal panes cut into the glass; the numerator is how many you may light — and a keeper may light only one. Knowing this lets the student aim a beam without guessing: read the bottom number, count the panes, confirm the glass matches, light one. The fraction symbol is literally the operating instruction for the lighthouse. In Mode B, the student's own writing commands a machine — engrave 1/8 and an eight-part lamp lights one eighth. Fraction notation stops being decoration and becomes the control language of the harbor.
artifact.stakes: Ships are inbound through fog on a timer-free but visible approach line. Each correctly lit lamp guides one ship into the harbor, where it docks and stays lit for the rest of the session, building a warmer and warmer skyline. A ship that receives a wrong signal doesn't sink or vanish — it circles back out into the fog and returns for another attempt, and the harbor stays a shade darker until it's brought in. The pressure is cumulative brightness, never loss.
artifact.consequences: Correct: the pane ignites, the beam sweeps, the ship's answering lamp appears, a dock light stays on permanently. Incorrect pane count awareness (student lights a pane on a lamp whose glass has the wrong number of divisions, in rounds offering a choice of lamps): the beam fires but disperses in the fog — the ship holds position and the glass shows a translucent overlay of how many panes the plate asked for versus how many the glass has. Incorrect engraving in Mode B: the twin lamp obeys the plate and visibly disagrees with the original — for example the original shows one of five lit and the twin shows one of three lit — and the two sit side by side until the student re-engraves. Nothing is marked with a red X; the mismatch is the feedback.
artifact.recovery: The keeper's lever can always be pulled to replay the anatomy animation. On a second miss in the same round, the glass helpfully numbers its panes 1, 2, 3… as they flash, so counting is offloaded. On a third miss, the round converts to guided mode (correct pane pulses again, or in Mode B the denominator slot is pre-filled and only the numerator remains), the student completes it, and the same denominator returns two rounds later un-guided so the recovered skill is retested rather than skipped. No round is failed out of; ships always come back.
progression: Beacon 1 — Halves and quarters, round glass only, correct pane pulsing then ghost-traced. Pure tap. Establishes 'bottom number = panes, light one'.
Beacon 2 — Denominators 2, 3, 4 across round, rectangular, and pier-bar lamps. No pulse, no ghost. Student must count panes before tapping.

Beacon 3 — Denominators 5 and 6 introduced; the same denominator appears on two differently shaped lamps in a row so the student sees 1/6 of a hexagon lantern and 1/6 of a long bar are both 'one of six'.
Beacon 4 — First Engrave the Plate rounds: lamp lit, plate blank, denominators 2 through 6. Twin-lamp verification active.
Beacon 5 — Denominators 7 and 8 in both modes; panes are visibly thinner, so careful counting matters more than eyeballing.

Beacon 6 — Mixed harbor: a row of three lamps arrives per round, each with its own plate, and the student services them in any order. Some lamps in the row are unequally divided decoys that spark and refuse to light.
Beacon 7 — Keeper's Night: alternating Light-the-Pane and Engrave-the-Plate with denominators 2 through 8 drawn without repeats, tracking the evidence tally to completion.
artifact.worldReaction: The harbor is a living scoreboard. Each guided ship becomes a permanent moored light; gulls settle on the pier as it brightens; fog thins band by band as the count of docked ships rises. The lighthouse itself gains detail — a brass railing, a weather vane, a keeper's cat asleep on the sill — at milestones. A wall chart inside the lamp room fills in with a small sketched shape for each denominator the student has mastered: a circle in halves, a bar in fifths, a hexagon in eighths, each with one part shaded and its symbol written beneath in the student's confirmed engraving.
artifact.payoff: When the last ship of the night docks, the fog clears entirely and the whole harbor is visible and lit. The keeper's wall chart lifts off the wall and becomes the Keeper's Card — a single printable/shareable page showing every unit fraction the student commanded, each as a shape with exactly one part shaded and the symbol beneath it, titled 'Keeper of the Harbor: reads and writes one of any number of equal parts.' The lighthouse beam then spells, in one slow sweep across the water, the phrase the student can now use anywhere: ONE PART OF EIGHT EQUAL PARTS IS ONE EIGHTH.
artifact.replayVariation: Each night generates a new harbor: different lamp shapes in the rotation (round glass, sash window, hexagonal signal lantern, pier bar-lamp, diamond storm lamp), different orientations (bars run horizontal or vertical, wedges start at different angles), different ship silhouettes and names, and a different weather mood (calm starlight, drifting fog, light rain that beads on the glass). Denominators are shuffled so the sequence never repeats, and the ratio of Light-the-Pane to Engrave-the-Plate rounds shifts toward engraving on repeat nights. A 'Storm Night' variant appears after two clears: wind rocks the lamp housing gently so panes rotate slowly, requiring the student to identify one of b equal parts on a moving wheel — same math, steadier hand.
artifact.visualDirection: Warm brass-and-glass nautical romanticism against deep indigo. The lamp housing is the hero object: thick beveled glass panes with visible mullions, drawn with clean 2–3px dark outlines so pane boundaries are unambiguous at a glance. Unlit panes are cool slate blue-grey; a lit pane is amber-white with a soft bloom and a faint lens-flare cross. Brass plates use an engraved serif numeral with a solid horizontal fraction bar the same weight as the mullions — visually rhyming the bar in 1/6 with the cuts in the glass. High contrast, no texture noise inside panes, so counting is easy. Distractor unequal-glass lamps are drawn with obviously mismatched pane widths, never subtly off. All shapes are large, centered, and touch-friendly; a colorblind-safe amber/slate pairing carries all state, with an added lit-pane checkmark stipple for redundancy.
artifact.motionDirection: Ignition is fast and satisfying: pane fills with light in 180ms with a slight overshoot bloom, then the beam sweeps outward across the water over 900ms. Pane counting animations flash each pane for 220ms in sequence with a soft tick, so counting is felt as rhythm. Wrong-engraving twin lamps slide in side by side over 400ms and hold — no shake, no flash. Ships glide, they never jerk. The lever pull has real weight: 120ms of resistance, a clunk, then release. Fog dissipates as a slow continuous parallax, always in the background, never distracting during a decision.
artifact.soundDirection: Harbor ambience: distant swell, rigging creak, an occasional gull. Correct ignition is a warm glass chime layered with a low resonant hum that swells as the beam sweeps. Pane-counting ticks are a small brass tap, pitched one step up per pane so eight panes make an ascending run the ear can count. Incorrect engraving produces no harsh sound — just the twin lamp's dull, off-key clunk of a mechanism doing exactly what it was told. Each docked ship adds one voice to a slowly building harmonic chord, so a full harbor literally sounds resolved. Optional keeper's voice reads each plate aloud once ('one sixth') to bind symbol to spoken name; toggleable.
usefulLibraries: SVG (inline, hand-authored) — exact geometric partitioning of circles, rectangles, hexagons, and bars into 2–8 provably equal parts with crisp tappable path hit-areas
GSAP — timeline control for ignition, sequential pane-count flashes, beam sweeps, and lever mechanics
Pixi.js — optional layer for fog, water shimmer, and beam bloom without touching the crisp SVG lamp geometry
Howler.js — layered ambience, pitched pane-tick sequence, and the cumulative docked-ship chord
Interact.js — drag-and-drop of brass numeral tiles into the fraction slots with forgiving snap targets
React (or plain state machine) — round sequencing, guided/unguided modes, recovery escalation, and evidence tallying
html2canvas — rendering the final Keeper's Card wall chart to a saveable image
artifact.engagementPrediction: Strong fit. The core loop is a single decisive act on a clearly bounded visual field — the same shape of task Reina has voluntarily repeated hundreds of times — but with a warm, accumulating world instead of a bare score. Her tolerance for imperfect accuracy in scanning tasks means the counting challenge at denominators 7–8 should read as interesting rather than defeating, while the no-red-X, ship-returns feedback model is designed to hold her frustration below the level her scanning history suggests. Expect high completion of a full night and voluntary replay for the alternate harbors; the Engrave-the-Plate mode is predicted to be her favorite because it casts her as the authority whose written mark the machine obeys, echoing the checking task she completed 167 times at perfect accuracy.
artifact.falsifyingEvidence: The design is wrong if: (1) she completes fewer than half the rounds in a night, or abandons during Beacon 1–2, indicating the tap loop is too thin without a word/language hook; (2) accuracy on Light-the-Pane stays high but Engrave-the-Plate accuracy collapses below ~50%, indicating the symbol-writing transfer isn't carried by the twin-lamp feedback and needs explicit scaffolding of the bar-and-numeral anatomy; (3) she taps repeatedly and rapidly across panes before confirming (guess-cycling) rather than counting, meaning the pane-count rhythm cue isn't being used and denominators 7–8 arrived too early; (4) frustration indicators exceed her word-radar baseline of 0.271 despite the soft-failure model, meaning the cumulative-brightness stakes are read as pressure rather than warmth; (5) she never pulls the anatomy lever after a miss, meaning recovery is invisible and must be pushed rather than offered.

node.responsibility: Compare two unit fractions with different denominators (e.g., 1/5 vs. 1/2) and justify which is larger based on the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.
node.academicBoundary: Limit to unit fraction comparisons only, using denominators 2 through 8, with same-size wholes. Do not introduce non-unit fraction comparisons, addition/subtraction of fractions, or equivalent fractions.
node.evidenceGoal: Student correctly compares at least 4 new pairs of unit fractions (using >, <, or =) and provides a correct reasoning statement (e.g., 'fewer equal parts means each part is bigger') for at least 3 of the comparisons.

artifact.title: Potion Split Showdown
artifact.audienceRationale: Reina's history shows huge engagement with rapid, high-repetition mastery loops (167 completions at perfect accuracy in a checking-style activity) plus enjoyment of chance-reveal spinners. Potion Split Showdown pairs a fast compare-and-verify loop with a spin-to-reveal challenge generator, feeding her love of precision streaks without copying any prior activity.
artifact.openingPromise: Two rival potion bottles, one gulp each — pick the bigger sip and out-brew the Shadow Alchemist.
artifact.firstThreeSeconds: A glowing cauldron room fades in. A brass reveal-wheel spins on its own and clunks to a stop, stamping two fraction cards onto the table: 1/3 and 1/6. A voice whispers: 'Bigger sip wins. Tap it.'
artifact.firstAction: Tap one of two identical-size potion bottles, each divided into a different number of equal doses (e.g., 3 doses vs. 6 doses) with exactly one dose glowing. The child taps the bottle whose single glowing dose looks bigger.
artifact.interactionDemonstration: A ghostly hand demos round zero: it taps 1/2 vs 1/8, the two bottles slide together and overlap transparently so the halves and eighths line up, showing the half-dose towering over the eighth-dose. A caption reads: 'Fewer parts → bigger parts.' No penalty on the demo.
artifact.coreInteraction: Each round: the reveal-wheel spins and lands on a fraction pair (denominators 2–8, same-size bottles). The child (1) taps the bigger sip or a 'same size' scale icon, (2) drags the correct symbol >, <, or = into the comparison slot between the fraction cards, and (3) picks or speaks a reasoning tile such as 'The whole is cut into fewer parts, so each part is bigger.' Bottles then overlay to visually verify the answer.
artifact.mathAsPower: Correct comparisons pour the bigger sip into Reina's cauldron, charging a Brew Meter. Correct reasoning statements add a 'Certainty Seal' that doubles the pour. The mathematics — knowing more parts means smaller parts — is literally the fuel that out-brews the rival.
artifact.stakes: The Shadow Alchemist's cauldron auto-fills slowly each round. If Reina's Brew Meter falls behind for three straight rounds, the Alchemist steals a Certainty Seal.
artifact.consequences: A wrong tap or wrong symbol triggers the overlay: bottles fuse and the parts align so the size difference is undeniable; the round scores no pour, but nothing is lost except tempo. Wrong reasoning tiles gray out with a one-line hint ('Count the parts — which bottle has fewer cuts?').
artifact.recovery: After any miss, a 'Re-Brew' round appears with the same denominators but the bottles pre-overlaid, letting Reina answer with visual support and reclaim half the pour. Stolen Seals are recoverable by winning two consecutive full rounds.
progression: Round set 1: far-apart denominators (1/2 vs 1/8, 1/3 vs 1/7) with bottles always visible and partitioned.
Round set 2: closer denominators (1/5 vs 1/6, 1/6 vs 1/8) plus occasional equal pairs (1/4 vs 1/4) to earn the '=' scale.
Round set 3: fraction cards shown first, bottles hidden until after the symbol is placed — compare from the numbers alone, then verify visually.
Boss Brew: five rapid comparisons with reasoning required on at least three to seal the Alchemist's cauldron shut.
artifact.worldReaction: The cauldron bubbles higher and changes color with each correct pour; potion imps cheer and chant the reasoning back ('Fewer cuts, bigger sip!'); the Shadow Alchemist visibly sweats as the meter gap grows.
artifact.payoff: Winning the Boss Brew crowns Reina 'Master of the Bigger Sip' and unlocks a trophy shelf showing her fastest correct streak and best reasoning statements — evidence of at least 4 correct comparisons and 3 justifications, satisfying the node goal.
artifact.replayVariation: The reveal-wheel reshuffles pairs each run; new potion themes (fire brew, moon brew) reskin bottles as bars or circles; a Speed Brew mode leans into streak-chasing; a Judge mode flips roles so Reina grades the imps' comparisons and fixes wrong symbols.
artifact.visualDirection: Cozy alchemist workshop: deep purples and teals, warm candlelight, glass bottles with luminous liquid doses, chunky rounded UI cards. Equal-size bottles are visually emphasized with matching gold rims.
artifact.motionDirection: Wheel spins with satisfying deceleration and clunk; bottle overlay is a smooth slide-and-fade alignment; correct pours arc liquid into the cauldron with a splash; Brew Meter rises with elastic easing.
artifact.soundDirection: Bubbling ambience, ratchet ticks on the wheel, a rich glug on correct pours, a soft glass 'tink' plus whispered hint on misses, rising choral shimmer as the Brew Meter nears full.
artifact.engagementPrediction: High: the loop mirrors her demonstrated appetite for fast, repeatable verification tasks with visible streaks, and the spinner reveal taps her wheel-of-fortune enjoyment. Expect long sessions chasing perfect Boss Brews.
artifact.falsifyingEvidence: If Reina answers by tapping visuals but repeatedly fails hidden-bottle rounds or skips/randomizes reasoning tiles (reasoning accuracy under ~60% across 10+ rounds), the design is masking guessing with visuals; if frustration events (rapid re-taps, quits after Seal theft) exceed her historical ~0.27 baseline, the stakes system is misfiring.
